items.prompt: What does 'blast radius' mean in this unit's terms?

The total number of servers a deploy touches, regardless of traffic
The physical distance between data centers running a service
The number of engineers who get paged during an incident
items.explanation: Blast radius is about exposure, not infrastructure footprint — it's how much real traffic or how many users a bad deploy reaches before something catches it, which is exactly what progressive-delivery's staged rollout is designed to limit.
items.reference:
💥 Blast radius = how much traffic a bad deploy reaches before it's caught
🕊️ progressive-delivery's canary is the tool for keeping it small

Why: Team B's 5% canary vs. Team A's 100% exposure is the whole difference in outcome.

0% — the deploy never reached any real traffic

items.reference:
💥 Blast radius = how much traffic a bad deploy reaches before it's caught
🕊️ progressive-delivery's canary is the tool for keeping it small

Why: Team B's 5% canary vs. Team A's 100% exposure is the whole difference in outcome.

⏱️ Detection latency = time from bad deploy live to someone noticing
📟 infra-observability's SLO-based alerting is what shrinks it

⏪ Safe reversibility = undo fast without causing a second incident

items.reference:
⏪ Safe reversibility = undo fast without causing a second incident

items.prompt: Complete `validateConfig(config, rules)`. Each rule has `key`, `required`, and an optional `validate(value)` function. Return `{ valid, errors }` where `errors` lists a message for each missing required key or failed `validate` check, and `valid` is true only when `errors` is empty.

tests.description: missing required key produces an error
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({}, [{ key: 'A', required: true }]).valid).toBe(false)

tests.description: value failing validate() produces an error
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({ A: 5 }, [{ key: 'A', required: true, validate: (v) => v > 10 }]).valid).toBe(false)

tests.description: valid config passes with no errors
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({ A: 20 }, [{ key: 'A', required: true, validate: (v) => v > 10 }])).toEqual({ valid: true, errors: [] })

tests.description: an optional, absent key with no validate rule does not produce an error
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({}, [{ key: 'B', required: false }]).valid).toBe(true)

items.explanation: This is Gate 1 of the pipeline: it walks every rule, flags a missing required key immediately (and skips the value-level check for it), and separately flags a present value that fails its own validate function — the deploy is only valid if neither kind of error was found.
items.reference:
🛂 Gate 1: reject missing required keys or out-of-range values
⏱️ Cheapest gate — runs before any traffic is served

Why: The earliest, cheapest gate catches a whole class of bug before it ever costs real traffic.

items.prompt: Complete `validateConfig(config, rules)`. Each rule has `key`, `required`, and an optional `validate(value)` function. Return `{ valid, errors }` where `errors` lists a message for each missing required key or failed `validate` check, and `valid` is true only when `errors` is empty.

tests.description: two rules, one missing, one failing validate -> 2 errors
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({ B: 1 }, [{ key: 'A', required: true }, { key: 'B', required: true, validate: (v) => v > 10 }]).errors.length).toBe(2)

tests.description: all rules satisfied -> valid true, no errors
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({ A: 'x', B: 20 }, [{ key: 'A', required: true }, { key: 'B', required: true, validate: (v) => v > 10 }])).toEqual({ valid: true, errors: [] })

tests.description: empty rules list is always valid
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({}, [])).toEqual({ valid: true, errors: [] })

tests.description: an empty-string value on a required key counts as missing
tests.expr: expect(validateConfig({ A: '' }, [{ key: 'A', required: true }]).valid).toBe(false)

items.explanation: Treating an empty string the same as a missing value for a required key catches the common real-world case of an env var being set but left blank, which is functionally the same failure as never setting it at all.
items.reference:
🛂 Gate 1: reject missing required keys or out-of-range values
⏱️ Cheapest gate — runs before any traffic is served

Why: The earliest, cheapest gate catches a whole class of bug before it ever costs real traffic.

items.prompt: Complete `isHealthy(snapshot, maxErrorRatePercent)` where `snapshot` is `{ requestCount, errorCount }`. Return `true` if `requestCount` is 0 (nothing to judge yet), otherwise return whether the error rate percent is at or below `maxErrorRatePercent`.

tests.description: 0 requests -> healthy (nothing observed yet)
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 0, errorCount: 0 }, 2)).toBe(true)

tests.description: 48/400 = 12% error rate, threshold 2% -> unhealthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 400, errorCount: 48 }, 2)).toBe(false)

tests.description: 4/2000 = 0.2% error rate, threshold 2% -> healthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 2000, errorCount: 4 }, 2)).toBe(true)

tests.description: exactly at the threshold counts as healthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 100, errorCount: 2 }, 2)).toBe(true)

items.explanation: A zero-request snapshot has nothing to judge yet, so it defaults to healthy rather than false-alarming on missing data; otherwise the observed error rate is compared inclusively against the threshold, matching the canary's actual pass/fail decision in runRelease.
items.reference:
📊 errorRatePercent = errorCount / requestCount × 100
✅ healthy = errorRatePercent ≤ maxErrorRatePercent

Why: This is the exact check that catches L1's bug at the 5% canary stage.

items.prompt: Complete `isHealthy(snapshot, maxErrorRatePercent)` where `snapshot` is `{ requestCount, errorCount }`. Return `true` if `requestCount` is 0 (nothing to judge yet), otherwise return whether the error rate percent is at or below `maxErrorRatePercent`.

tests.description: 10/1000 = 1% error rate, threshold 2% -> healthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 1000, errorCount: 10 }, 2)).toBe(true)

tests.description: 30/1000 = 3% error rate, threshold 2% -> unhealthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 1000, errorCount: 30 }, 2)).toBe(false)

tests.description: 0 requests with a very strict threshold is still healthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 0, errorCount: 0 }, 0.1)).toBe(true)

tests.description: all requests failing is unhealthy
tests.expr: expect(isHealthy({ requestCount: 50, errorCount: 50 }, 2)).toBe(false)

items.explanation: The check simplifies to one comparison once the zero-request edge case is handled: compute the percent, then allow anything at or under the configured maximum, exactly the same rule the orchestrator relies on when deciding whether a canary stage should proceed or trigger rollback.
items.reference:
📊 errorRatePercent = errorCount / requestCount × 100
✅ healthy = errorRatePercent ≤ maxErrorRatePercent

Why: This is the exact check that catches L1's bug at the 5% canary stage.

items.prompt: Given working `validateConfig` and `isHealthy` functions (already defined), complete `runRelease(input)`'s canary loop: for each stage in `input.canaryStages`, call `input.observeHealth(stage.trafficPercent)`, check health with `isHealthy`, and if unhealthy call `input.rollback()` and return `{ status: 'rolled-back', failedAtPercent: stage.trafficPercent }` immediately. If every stage is healthy, return `{ status: 'shipped-to-100' }`.

tests.description: unhealthy first stage triggers rollback and stops before later stages
tests.expr: let called = false; expect(runRelease({ config: {}, configRules: [], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }, { trafficPercent: 100 }], observeHealth: (p) => p === 5 ? { requestCount: 400, errorCount: 48 } : { requestCount: 1, errorCount: 1 }, maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => { called = true; } }).status).toBe('rolled-back')

tests.description: all healthy stages -> shipped-to-100
tests.expr: expect(runRelease({ config: {}, configRules: [], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }, { trafficPercent: 100 }], observeHealth: () => ({ requestCount: 1000, errorCount: 1 }), maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => {} }).status).toBe('shipped-to-100')

tests.description: rollback() is actually invoked on an unhealthy stage
tests.expr: let called = false; runRelease({ config: {}, configRules: [], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }], observeHealth: () => ({ requestCount: 100, errorCount: 50 }), maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => { called = true; } }); expect(called).toBe(true)

tests.description: failedAtPercent matches the stage that failed
tests.expr: expect(runRelease({ config: {}, configRules: [], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 25 }], observeHealth: () => ({ requestCount: 100, errorCount: 50 }), maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => {} }).failedAtPercent).toBe(25)

items.explanation: The loop is the pipeline's Gates 2 through 4 as code: observe health at each stage, and on the first unhealthy result, call rollback() and return immediately rather than continuing to expose more traffic — this is exactly the branch that catches L1's bug at 5% instead of letting it reach 100%.
items.reference:
🔁 Loop each stage: observe → check health → rollback + return on failure
🏁 Reaching the end of the loop with no failures means shipped-to-100

Why: One reachable early-return branch is the entire difference between Team A and Team B's afternoon.

items.prompt: Given working `validateConfig` and `isHealthy` functions (already defined), complete `runRelease(input)`'s canary loop: for each stage in `input.canaryStages`, call `input.observeHealth(stage.trafficPercent)`, check health with `isHealthy`, and if unhealthy call `input.rollback()` and return `{ status: 'rolled-back', failedAtPercent: stage.trafficPercent }` immediately. If every stage is healthy, return `{ status: 'shipped-to-100' }`.

tests.description: invalid config never reaches the canary loop at all
tests.expr: let observed = false; expect(runRelease({ config: { __forceInvalid: true }, configRules: [{}], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }], observeHealth: () => { observed = true; return { requestCount: 1, errorCount: 0 }; }, maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => {} }).status).toBe('rejected-invalid-config')

tests.description: canary is never observed when config is invalid
tests.expr: let observed = false; runRelease({ config: { __forceInvalid: true }, configRules: [{}], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }], observeHealth: () => { observed = true; return { requestCount: 1, errorCount: 0 }; }, maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => {} }); expect(observed).toBe(false)

tests.description: valid config with a single healthy stage ships to 100
tests.expr: expect(runRelease({ config: {}, configRules: [], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }], observeHealth: () => ({ requestCount: 500, errorCount: 0 }), maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => {} }).status).toBe('shipped-to-100')

tests.description: multiple healthy stages all still ship to 100
tests.expr: expect(runRelease({ config: {}, configRules: [], canaryStages: [{ trafficPercent: 5 }, { trafficPercent: 25 }, { trafficPercent: 100 }], observeHealth: () => ({ requestCount: 500, errorCount: 0 }), maxErrorRatePercent: 2, rollback: () => {} }).status).toBe('shipped-to-100')

items.explanation: Because the config check returns before the loop ever starts, an invalid config never triggers even a single observeHealth call — this is the concrete proof that Gate 1 is strictly earlier and cheaper than letting the canary discover the same problem.
